patterns.title: MSI launch condition blocked the install
patterns.summary: The package's LaunchConditions check failed, so Windows Installer refused to start. This is a deliberate gate in the MSI (OS version, CPU architecture, a missing runtime, or a newer version already present), not a crash.

remediation.detail: Look a few lines above the failing line for the message the installer tried to show (it usually names the missing requirement).
Install or deploy the requirement first, then retry. In Intune, model it as an app dependency so it installs automatically.
Run the MSI interactively as SYSTEM or admin with verbose logging to see the exact message.

patterns.title: MSI custom action failed
regex: CustomAction (?P<detail>\S+ returned actual error code \d+)(?!.*translated to success)
patterns.summary: A custom action inside the installer returned an error and it was not marked as ignorable, so the install stopped. The action name tells you which stage broke ({detail}).

remediation.detail: Search the log for the action name and read the 20-30 lines before it; the cause is usually logged just ahead of the failure.

remediation.action: Check what the action depends on
remediation.detail: Custom actions typically run scripts, check prerequisites or start services. Confirm those are present for the SYSTEM account.
Reproduce with verbose logging on a test device in the same context (SYSTEM) as Intune.

patterns.title: MSI action returned failure (Return value 3)
patterns.summary: The installer action '{detail}' failed. 'Return value 3' is how a verbose MSI log marks the first step that went wrong; everything after it is clean-up and rollback.

remediation.action: Read the lines above the failing action
remediation.detail: The reason is normally logged immediately before 'Return value 3'.
Reproduce as SYSTEM so you see what Intune sees.

patterns.title: Windows Installer reported the operation failed
patterns.summary: Windows Installer ended the operation for '{detail}' as failed. This is the outcome, not the reason - look for the cause earlier in the log.

remediation.detail: Find the first 'Return value 3' or error before it.

patterns.title: MSI finished with a non-zero status
patterns.summary: The installer's final status was {detail}. Intune and Patch My PC treat anything other than 0, 1707, 3010 or 1641 as a failure.

remediation.detail: Match the number against the Windows Installer error code list and read the lines before the final status.

patterns.title: Windows Installer raised a numbered error
patterns.summary: The installer logged a numbered error: {detail}

remediation.action: Act on the specific error number
remediation.detail: The error number identifies the failing condition. See the code meaning in the finding and the Windows Installer error codes reference.

patterns.title: Installer requested a restart
patterns.summary: The install finished but needs a restart (3010 = soft reboot, 1641 = installer started a reboot). That is not a failure, but a pending restart can block the next installer.

remediation.action: Map the return code in Intune
remediation.detail: Make sure 3010 is set to 'Soft reboot' (or Hard reboot if you want one) in the app's return codes.
Use a restart grace period or maintenance window so users are not surprised.

patterns.title: Another installation was already running (1618)
regex: another installation is already in progress
patterns.summary: Windows Installer only runs one install at a time and the mutex was held by something else (another MSI, Windows Update, or a second Intune/Patch My PC job).

remediation.detail: Usually clears on its own. Intune retries failed Win32 apps automatically.
Check which msiexec.exe or TrustedInstaller.exe process is running and why.
Stagger assignments so Patch My PC, Windows Update and Intune apps do not all land at the same moment.

patterns.title: MSI package could not be opened (1619/1620)
regex: This installation package could not be opened
patterns.summary: Windows Installer could not open the .msi file. Typical reasons: a truncated or corrupt download, the file is on a path SYSTEM cannot reach, or security software locked or removed it.

remediation.detail: Confirm the file hash matches the source and the package was not modified after upload.
Make sure the MSI is local when it runs (Intune stages it in the IME cache) and not on a UNC share SYSTEM cannot read.
Look for Defender or EDR detections on the file around the time of the failure.

patterns.title: Installer source is not available (1612/1706)
regex: installation source for this product is not available
No valid source could be found
patterns.summary: Windows Installer needs the original MSI to repair, upgrade or uninstall this product and cannot find it. This is common when the cached package was cleaned up.

remediation.detail: Upgrade or uninstall using the same MSI version that was originally installed, or use the Microsoft Program Install and Uninstall troubleshooter.
If the product is gone but still registered, remove the orphaned entry (for example with the Microsoft Install/Uninstall troubleshooter or msizap-style tooling) and reinstall.

patterns.title: Another or newer version is already installed (1638)
regex: Another version of this product is already installed
A newer version of .{0,80} is already installed
patterns.summary: The MSI will not install over the version already on the device (same product, different version, no major upgrade defined).

remediation.detail: Use a pre-install script, a supersedence relationship in Intune, or the vendor's uninstall switch.

remediation.action: Check the product and upgrade codes
remediation.detail: If the vendor ships a major upgrade, the new MSI should replace the old one; if not, they need to be removed explicitly.

patterns.title: Installer lacked privileges (1925)
regex: do not have sufficient privileges to complete this installation
patterns.summary: The install ran without administrator rights for an all-users install.

remediation.action: Set the install context to System
remediation.detail: In the Intune Win32 app, set Install behaviour to 'System' rather than 'User'.
If run through a script, make sure it runs as SYSTEM or elevated.

patterns.title: A service failed to start or install (1920)
patterns.summary: The installer tried to start a service as part of setup and it did not come up. The service itself usually logs why in the Windows Event Log.

remediation.action: Check the service account and dependencies
remediation.detail: Confirm the service's logon account, dependencies and binary path are valid.
Look in System and Application logs around the failure time.
EDR or AppLocker rules sometimes stop new services starting.

patterns.title: Installer could not write a file or folder (1303/1304/1310/1321)
patterns.summary: The installer was refused access to a file or folder while copying files.

remediation.detail: Confirm SYSTEM has write access and the folder is not redirected or locked.
A running copy of the app, or an AV scan, may hold the file open.
Defender Controlled Folder Access or ASR rules can block writes to protected locations.

patterns.title: MSI script custom action failed (1722)
patterns.summary: A program or script run by the installer did not finish as expected.

remediation.detail: Find the 'Action start ... CustomAction' just before the failure and note which script or executable it runs.
Run the same script under SYSTEM (PsExec -s) to see the real error.

patterns.title: Installer failed registering a .NET assembly (1935)
regex: An error occurred during the installation of assembly
patterns.summary: Registering a .NET assembly in the GAC failed. Common causes are a damaged .NET Framework, a pending reboot or a stuck Windows servicing operation.

remediation.detail: A pending reboot often clears this.
Run DISM and SFC, then retry.

patterns.title: Windows Installer policy blocks the install (1625)
patterns.summary: A Windows Installer policy (DisableMSI, or an AppLocker/WDAC rule on installers) prevents this package from installing.

remediation.detail: Look at the DisableMSI value and any AppLocker Windows Installer rules.
Add a publisher or path rule, or sign the package with an allowed certificate.

patterns.title: Windows Installer service not accessible (1601)
regex: Windows Installer service could not be accessed
patterns.summary: The Windows Installer service is missing, disabled or damaged.

patterns.title: Temp folder is full or inaccessible (1632)
regex: Temp folder is either full or inaccessible
patterns.summary: Windows Installer could not use its temp folder.

remediation.action: Check free space and permissions on the temp path
remediation.detail: For SYSTEM this is C:\Windows\Temp.

patterns.title: Fatal error during installation (1603)
patterns.summary: 1603 is Windows Installer's catch-all failure. It says the install failed, not why - the reason is earlier in the log.

remediation.detail: Search the log for 'Return value 3' and read upwards.

patterns.title: Setup aborted itself (1602)
patterns.summary: 1602 means 'user cancelled', but setup bootstrappers also use it when they deliberately abort - for example when a prerequisite check fails in silent mode.

remediation.detail: Read the lines just before the abort for a 'needs to be installed' or 'not supported' message.
